paras: The expulsion of Bob Williamson from Cordale, Georgia, was an attack on a traveling picture salesman by white people who objected to his selling photographs of Sergeant Henry Johnson, reported in a dispatch dated April 4, 1919. Williamson's pictures were torn up, a pistol was put in his mouth, and he was ordered to leave town, which he did. The Chicago Defender carried the story on its front page as an example of Southern hostility to images of Black soldiers' war service.

Williamson was a traveling representative of a picture company selling photographs that, in the Defender's description, showed Sergeant Henry Johnson of the 15th New York killing several Germans in hand-to-hand combat in No Man's Land. According to the dispatch, white people in the town objected to the sale of these pictures.

Williamson received what the paper called a "mysterious telephone call" asking him to bring his pictures for inspection to an art store "located in a white settlement." When he arrived, his pictures were overturned and torn to shreds. The muzzle of a pistol was then poked into his mouth and he was told to leave town immediately; the Defender reported that "Williamson obeyed." The dispatch names none of the attackers and does not say how many there were.
No report of arrests or of any official response appears in the coverage.

The only report found ran on page one of the Chicago Defender on April 5, 1919, under the headline "SELLER OF WAR PICTURES." The Defender set the incident in a wider pattern, adding that "in some portions of Georgia, Florida and Mississippi the law strictly forbids" the sale of pictures of "the gallant deeds of our soldiers." The dispatch does not state Williamson's race, and no other Black paper was found to have carried the story.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender dispatch
accounts.gist: White people in Cordale who objected to photographs of Sergeant Henry Johnson lured salesman Bob Williamson to an art store by telephone, tore his pictures, put a pistol in his mouth and ordered him out of town; he left.

framing.detail: The Defender ran it on page one under "SELLER OF WAR PICTURES", called Johnson's feat one of "the gallant deeds of our soldiers", and said selling such pictures was claimed to be forbidden in parts of three Southern states.
